title: Solving General-Utility Markov Decision Processes in the Single-Trial Regime with Online Planning
claim: Different utility objectives on small, shared-dynamics decision processes require different single-trial behavior, illustrated with concrete toy instances.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: two state-transition graphs, then a bar chart
description: Three panels show small example decision processes. Panel (a) is a three-state graph with states 1, 0 and 2 drawn as circles. Arrows are labelled with actions a0 and a1, and self-loops sit on states 1 and 2. An entry arrow points into state 0 from below. This graph is shared by the entropy-maximization GUMDP M_f,1 and the adversarial-MDP GUMDP M_f,3. Panel (b) is a two-state graph with states 1 and 0 and the same action labels. It is for the imitation-learning GUMDP M_f,2. Panel (c) is a grouped bar chart of cost against six state-action pairs, from (s0,a0) to (s2,a1). Each pair has three bars for c1 (orange), c2 (blue) and c3 (red), with cost values from 0.5 to 2.0. The eye goes first to the colorful bars on the right. The graphs are black-and-white line drawings.
caption: Illustrative GUMDPs. Mf,1 and Mf,3 share the same dynamics but differ in the objective function. In all GUMDPs, the chosen action succeeds with 90% probability and, with 10% probability, the agent randomly moves to any of the states. The behavior policy for Mf,2 is β(a0|s0) = 0.8 and β(a0|s1) = 0.2. In (c), we plot the three cost functions, c1, c2 and c3, of the adversarial MDP.
abstract: In this work, we contribute the first approach to solve infinite-horizon discounted general-utility Markov decision processes (GUMDPs) in the single-trial regime, i.e., when the agent's performance is evaluated based on a single trajectory. First, we provide some fundamental results regarding policy optimization in the single-trial regime, investigating which class of policies suffices for optimality, casting our problem as a particular MDP that is equivalent to our original problem, as well as studying the computational hardness of policy optimization in the single-trial regime. Second, we show how we can leverage online planning techniques, in particular a Monte-Carlo tree search algorithm, to solve GUMDPs in the single-trial regime. Third, we provide experimental results showcasing the superior performance of our approach in comparison to relevant baselines.
